questions.topic: Repeated input with a shared output
questions.learningObjective: explain why a shared output is allowed
questions.stem: Ticket OPS-123 asks why a rule may send two different inputs to the same output and still be a function. Explain it.

answer.exemplar: A function only requires that each input has exactly one output, so nothing stops two different inputs from sharing an output value. For example the rule f of x equals x squared minus 4 sends the input 5 to 21 and also sends the input negative 5 to 21, and no input in that rule ever produces two different outputs, so it is a function. The repeated output does show that the rule is not one-to-one, which is a separate property, and it is that failure of one-to-one-ness that blocks an inverse function.

questions.explanation: The definition restricts outputs per input, not inputs per output, so a shared output is harmless. It only shows the rule is not one-to-one, which blocks an inverse.
questions.hint: Ask how many outputs one single input may carry.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.topic: Function defined on part of a number line
questions.learningObjective: explain the domain of a partly published rule
questions.stem: Ticket OPS-136 asks you to explain what the domain of a rule published only over part of the number line means.

answer.exemplar: The domain of a rule is the set of inputs for which the rule actually gives an output, so a rule published only over part of the number line has exactly that piece as its domain. If a rate limiter publishes a formula for request rates from 5 up to and including 100, then the domain is that closed interval and nothing outside it, because outside it no formula has been given. This is different from saying what happens to the other inputs, such as passing them through unchanged, since that statement is about behaviour and not about a rule that can be evaluated. A column of input values in a table of values is another way of publishing the same domain.

questions.explanation: A domain records where a rule can be evaluated, so a rule published over part of the number line has that piece as its domain and nothing more.
questions.hint: The domain is where the rule can actually be evaluated.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.learningObjective: explain the even property and its graph
questions.stem: The notes filed on ticket OPS-148 ask you to explain how a rule can be even and how that shows on a graph.

answer.exemplar: A rule is even when the value at a negated input equals the value at the input itself, which for a polynomial means every term has an even power, since an even power keeps its value under negation and an odd power changes sign. Take the rule f of x equals 2x squared plus 7: the input 4 gives 2 times 16 plus 7, which is 39, and the input negative 4 gives exactly the same 39. On a graph this shows up as mirror symmetry about the vertical axis, because the height at a point to the left of the axis matches the height at the mirrored point to the right. The practical value of evenness is that a computation at a positive input can be reused for the negative one.

questions.explanation: Evenness means negating the input changes nothing, which on a graph appears as mirror symmetry about the vertical axis. A rule with one odd power term fails the test.
questions.hint: Compare the values at an input and at its negative.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.learningObjective: explain oddness and its graph
questions.stem: A reviewer working through ticket OPS-160 asks you to explain what it means for a rule to be odd and what its graph looks like.

answer.exemplar: A rule is odd when the value at a negated input is the negative of the value at the input, so the whole output changes sign when the input does. For a polynomial this happens when every term has an odd power and there is no constant term, because odd powers change sign and a constant does not. Take f of x equals 3x cubed minus x: the input 2 gives 3 times 8 minus 2, which is 22, and the input negative 2 gives negative 22. On a graph the effect is a half turn of symmetry about the origin, and in particular the rule must take the value 0 at the input 0, since a number equal to its own negative can only be zero. That is a quick way to test a candidate rule.

questions.explanation: Oddness means the output flips sign with the input, which on a graph is a half turn about the origin and forces the value at 0 to be 0. A constant term ruins it.
questions.hint: Check the value at zero and the sign at a negative input.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.learningObjective: explain what the horizontal line test shows
questions.stem: For ticket OPS-172 you are asked to explain what the horizontal line test tells you about a rule and why that matters.

answer.exemplar: The horizontal line test asks whether any horizontal line can meet the graph of a rule more than once, and a line meeting twice means that one output value is produced by two different inputs. A rule can still be a function in that case, because the function rule only restricts how many outputs one input may have, but it is not one-to-one, and a one-to-one rule is exactly what is needed for an inverse function to exist. The test is the geometric version of asking whether the equation for the output has more than one solution for a given input value. Take the rule f of x equals x squared on the whole real line: the horizontal line at the height 4 meets the graph at the input 2 and at the input negative 2, so the rule has no inverse function, while the same rule restricted to inputs of 0 and above passes the test and does.

questions.explanation: The horizontal line test detects an output shared by two inputs, so it settles one-to-one-ness rather than whether the rule is a function. That is the property an inverse needs.
questions.hint: Ask what a shared output says about reversing the rule.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.learningObjective: explain the mirror image of an inverse graph
questions.stem: A reviewer on ticket OPS-185 asks you to explain why the graph of an inverse is a mirror image across the line y equals x.

answer.exemplar: An inverse function undoes the original, so the point with the input a and the output b on the original graph becomes the point with the input b and the output a on the inverse graph. The set of all points that have their coordinates exchanged is exactly the mirror image across the line y equals x, because that line is the set of points whose two coordinates are equal, and a mirror across it sends a point to the point with the coordinates swapped. Take the rule f of x equals 2x plus 1, whose graph passes through the points 0 and 1, and 2 and 5. The inverse graph therefore passes through 1 and 0, and 5 and 2, which is the same picture reflected across the diagonal. A reflection across an axis would be a different operation, since it would negate one coordinate and leave the other alone.

questions.explanation: Each point's coordinates swap when a rule is reversed, and that swap is the reflection across the line y equals x. Reflecting across an axis negates one coordinate instead.
questions.hint: Follow one plotted point and watch its coordinates trade places.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.learningObjective: explain the quotient of two rules
questions.stem: For ticket OPS-193 you are asked to explain what the quotient of two function rules means and where it stops being defined.

answer.exemplar: The quotient of two rules divides the value of the first by the value of the second at the same input, so with f of x equals 4x minus 2 and g of x equals x plus 1 the quotient is the quantity 4x minus 2 over the quantity x plus 1. Because the denominator may be zero, the quotient is not defined at every input: here g equals 0 when x plus 1 equals 0, that is at the input negative 1, so that input is removed from the domain and the quotient has a domain of all real numbers except negative 1. Dividing the two values at an input is the same as evaluating this single rule, which is the pointwise definition, and it is also why the order of the two rules matters, since dividing by g is not the same as dividing by f.

questions.explanation: The quotient of two rules divides their values at the same input, and the denominator may vanish, removing that input from the domain. The order of the rules matters.
questions.hint: Ask what happens when the lower rule gives zero.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.learningObjective: explain the pointwise sum of two rules
questions.stem: The write-up for ticket OPS-205 asks you to explain how the sum of two function rules is computed and why the order does not matter.

answer.exemplar: The sum of two rules is computed pointwise: the same input goes into each rule and the two resulting outputs are added. With f of x equals 3x minus 2 and g of x equals x squared, the sum at the input 4 is 3 times 4 minus 2, which is 10, plus 4 squared, which is 16, giving 26. Writing the single rule 3x plus x squared minus 2 gives the same figure at 4, and it works for every input, not just this one. The order of the two terms in that single rule does not matter, because addition is commutative, so the sum of f and g is the same function as the sum of g and f. This is what makes the sum a genuine function: one input still produces exactly one output.

questions.explanation: The sum of two rules adds their values at the same input, and the two terms may be written in either order because addition is commutative. One input still gives one output.
questions.hint: Both rules use the same input, and the values are added.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.learningObjective: explain the pointwise product of two rules
questions.stem: The notes for ticket OPS-217 ask you to explain how the product of two function rules is computed and why it is useful to the team.

answer.exemplar: The product of two rules multiplies their values at the same input, so with f of x equals x plus 5 and g of x equals 2x minus 3, the product at the input 4 is 9 times 5, which is 45, and writing the single rule for the product gives the same figure for every input, not just for this one. The point of combining rules this way is that a quantity built from two separate measurements, such as a number of users and a price per user, can be tracked by one function, so that a change in either measurement shows up in the total without anyone re-deriving the arithmetic. The order of the two rules does not matter for a product, since multiplying is commutative, although the pairing of the same input does matter.

questions.explanation: A product of two rules multiplies their values at the same input, and it lets the team track two separate measurements as one function. The order of the factors does not matter.
questions.hint: Multiply the two values taken at the same input.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.learningObjective: explain why shared outputs matter to a team
questions.stem: A note for ticket OPS-229 asks you to explain why a team should care how many inputs reach the same output.

answer.exemplar: When two different inputs reach the same output, the rule is not one-to-one, and that single fact decides several practical questions. First, no inverse function can exist for the rule, because an inverse would have to send that one output back to two different inputs, which no function can do. Second, a lookup that assumes one input per output will be wrong for one of the two inputs, so a cache or a database key built on the output has to record that the value was reached twice. Third, a line drawn on a graph will be met twice by a horizontal line at that height, which is the geometric sign of the same fact. The rule itself stays a perfectly good function throughout, because a function only restricts how many outputs one input may have.

questions.explanation: Several inputs sharing one output means the rule is not one-to-one, which blocks an inverse and can break a lookup built on unique outputs. The rule itself is still a function.
questions.hint: Ask what an inverse or a lookup key would do with it.
